name: borsel
author: rule-family designer (dice)
description: DICE RULE-FAMILY class (docs/RULE_FAMILIES.md). Clue = 2 or 3 example rolls of k dice (k=3,4 or 5, fixed within a clue, pips space-separated, one roll per line, dice in random order). Answer = one more roll of k dice satisfying the hidden rule, and NOT a re-ordering of an example (the scorer compares sorted multisets). The hidden rule is drawn from a universe U of 10 templates / 22-23 concrete rules (k-dependent), all order-independent and all sayable by a kid in one breath: (0) the dice add up to exactly n, n in {3k-2,3k,3k+2,3k+4}; (1) the dice add up to more than 4k+2; (2) the dice add up to less than 3k-2; (3) the biggest die is m, m in {3,4}; (4) the smallest die is m, m in {3,4}; (5) exactly two of the dice show v, v in 1..6; (6) there are exactly i different numbers, i in 1..min(k-2,2); (7) the two biggest dice add up to s, s in {k+3,k+4}; (8) the two smallest dice add up to s, s in {10-k,11-k}; (9) the biggest die is double the smallest. Every parameter value was chosen so that the rule's probability under a uniform roll is 0.03-0.17 (mean 0.10), which is the answer rate of a player who guesses at random. generate() draws a rule, then a MINIMAL identifying example set: the examples together leave exactly one rule of U alive, and no proper subset does; it prefers a minimal 3-set and falls back to a minimal pair (measured: 30% three examples, 70% two). DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED templates (never the rule, frequently consistent with the examples - this is the trap the class teaches): 'every die is at least m' (consistent 100% of the time, scores 14%), 'no die is bigger than m' (100%, 12%), 'the total is odd/even' (60%, 6%), 'exactly c of the dice are odd' (31%, 6%), 'two of the dice add up to seven' (18%, 12%), 'there is a six' (18%, 12%), 'all the dice are odd / all even' (10%, 3%), 'the dice are in increasing order' (10%, 5%), 'all the dice are different' (1%), 'three of them are in a row' (2%). Note that the class only ever uses TIGHT statements (exactly m, exactly two vs at least m, at most m): the loose cousins of its own templates are the strongest traps. Foothold: copying an example with one die changed scores 26%; a random roll scores 8%; guessing 'same total as example 1' scores 29%. A player who has mapped U exactly scores 100%; a player who has mapped all but the two rarest templates scores 91%; a player who knows U but picks the wrong survivor scores 19%. solve() enumerates the rolls satisfying the unique survivor and returns a random one in random dice order.
solve:
def U_of(k):
    return ([(0, n) for n in (3*k-2, 3*k, 3*k+2, 3*k+4)]
        + [(1, 4*k+2), (2, 3*k-2), (9, 0)]
        + [(3, m) for m in (3, 4)]
        + [(4, m) for m in (3, 4)]
        + [(5, v) for v in range(1, 7)]
        + [(6, i) for i in range(1, min(k-1, 3))]
        + [(7, s) for s in (k+3, k+4)]
        + [(8, s) for s in (10-k, 11-k)])

def P(r, d):
    t, q = r
    S = sum(d)
    return [S == q, S > q, S < q, d[-1] == q, d[0] == q, d.count(q) == 2,
            len(set(d)) == q, d[-1]+d[-2] == q, d[0]+d[1] == q, d[-1] == 2*d[0]][t]

def solve(clue):
    E = [tuple(sorted(int(x) for x in l.split())) for l in clue.strip().split("\n")]
    k = len(E[0])
    V = [r for r in U_of(k) if all(P(r, e) for e in E)]
    ok = [d for d in itertools.combinations_with_replacement(range(1, 7), k)
          if P(V[0], d) and d not in E]
    r = random.Random(clue)
    d = list(r.choice(ok))          # a random valid roll, never a canonical one
    r.shuffle(d)                    # and in random order, like the examples
    return " ".join(map(str, d))
